change.title: Phase 6: Model II customer release within the NCC campaign
change.reason: Keep the 4 June 1979 Model II prototype demonstration and the 15 October customer release distinct. The existing NCC 1979 campaign already runs through January 1980 and explicitly promotes autumn Tandy deliveries; give it sole ownership of the public release instead of creating a new campaign or moving the whole engineering cooperation. Retain Tandy implementation and qualification responsibilities in its cooperation process, with technical deliverable outcomes unchanged. Assign the Model II Abacus product its campaign and October launch event, remove only the corresponding redundant reverse product references, and make the delivery-promotion event depend directly on the customer release. Remove scenario commentary and pricing-comparison wording from the touched release description. All event dates, process periods, technical definitions, compositions and current authorizations stay unchanged until review. Existing external-product release references remain necessary because external products have no product-owned launch fields. Remaining commercial-specification cleanup and the four other unresolved offerings remain for the catalogue closeout.

before.title: NCC 1979 open architecture and migration campaign
before.objective: Encourage independent manufacturers and developers to adopt documented compatibility interfaces, and show customers how supported software, documents and peripherals can protect their investment across computer brands.
audience: Business customers choosing computers, applications and peripherals.
Independent computer and peripheral manufacturers evaluating compatibility programmes.
Software publishers, developers, dealers and integrators supporting existing and future systems.
message: Choose your computer. Keep your investment.
Use documented interfaces and qualified configurations to connect products from independent suppliers.
Choose CP/M applications, FlexiBUS peripherals and display options separately; adopting one does not require the entire Logix platform.
Prepare for future computers through portable C source and documented interfaces while continuing to use and support established eight-bit systems.
claim_policy: Identify shipping products, qualified configurations, prototypes and plans separately. Manufacturer interest and campaign targets are not signed agreements, verified adoption or sales.

CP/M remains commercially licensed. Non-exclusive implementation rights do not change software ownership or imply open-source licensing. Reference-code rights, certification scope and support terms must be stated before making firm offers.
Claim compatibility only for named software versions, resources, host adapters and tested configurations. Preserve each supplier’s brand, licences and support responsibilities.
Label the Model II demonstration as a prototype until customer release. AION supplies the June 1979 cards; SMC remains a future source subject to individual chip qualification.

Apple’s demonstration participation covers native Apple II products and does not endorse S-100 systems. These products provide neither Apple CP/M/Z80 execution nor automatic conversion of existing Apple graphics.

Until 19 May 1980, refer to future systems only as next-generation computers. Withhold product, processor and OS names; word size, ISA, registers, execution design, address and memory organisation; performance figures, clock rates, chip counts, schematics, board images, bus topology and future display specifications.

Keep coprocessor implementation and integration details, future-target SDKs, compiler output, binaries and revealing benchmarks confidential. Apply this embargo to presentations, questions, advertising, dealer scripts, sales proposals, OEM briefings, clinics and all attachments; current CP/M, FlexiBUS and optional display documentation may be shared.

Use released eight-bit software and explicitly identified qualified prototypes in demonstrations. Label prepared data and recordings, obtain partner clearance, and report measured resource and interoperability limits rather than implying universal performance.
Do not imply an engineering guarantee, product withdrawal date or promise that every model remains in production. Do not promise funded support for an unspecified duration.

stage.label: Customer choice
stage.description: Explain how independent software, peripheral and display choices can protect a customer’s investment.

stage.label: Applications across computers
stage.description: Demonstrate an Abacus document round trip between Aurelia and the Model II prototype using separately qualified host editions. Show supported common behaviour without promising identical binaries or disk formats.

stage.label: Business applications
stage.description: Demonstrate Abacus, then independent BPI records and summary export. Explain the prepared data and separate licensing; do not imply that BPI has a Model II port.

stage.label: FlexiBUS peripherals
stage.description: Operate a qualified peripheral sequentially on named hosts. Show identification, driver support and supported application functions, attaching only when the port is quiescent.

stage.label: Apple II and S-100 expansion products
stage.description: Present the Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II alongside the S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. An Apple representative joins the native Apple demonstration. Explain the drivers, optional display hardware and separate S-100 support without suggesting Apple endorses S-100 systems.

stage.label: Independent partners
stage.description: DRI, Tandy, Microsoft, BPI management and confirmed peripheral participants explain their responsibilities and commercial access. Distinguish current AION chip supply from prospective SMC supply and signed partners from recruitment prospects.

stage.label: Preparing for the next generation
stage.description: Adam explains that future computers will not run existing Z80 binaries natively. Existing C tools and documented APIs reduce source migration work; recompilation, adaptation and testing remain necessary. Describe the planned optional Z80 coprocessor and the continuing role of eight-bit systems without revealing the new architecture.

stage.label: Availability and next steps
stage.description: Identify available products, prototypes and future plans. Direct customers and developers to documented configurations, licence terms, the compatibility directory and programme registration.

marketing_content.description: Specify the CP/M core and optional extension versions, processor instruction set, available transient-program memory, adapters and qualified applications for each configuration. Document common file formats and APIs. FlexiBUS and Logix video are optional; native displays, disks and conventional ports remain valid. Ordinary CP/M support does not guarantee every extended application, Z80 binary, file system or floppy format.

Publish electrical and transport rules, device-class profiles, host drivers, diagnostics and named qualification results. Other processors and operating systems may use their own drivers without adopting CP/M or Logix video. Device identification alone does not prove feature compatibility. Version 1 uses one device per point-to-point port, with no passive hub or daisy chain; its faster rate allows at most 50 KB/s before protocol overhead.

Separate graphics API compatibility from controller cards, the digital monitor link and qualified display modes. FlexiBUS and the full Aurelia architecture are optional. An 80-column mode needs a qualified 640-pixel monitor; adding a card does not give existing 320-pixel launch monitors that resolution.

marketing_content.type: Apple II and S-100 product sheet
marketing_content.description: The NCC launch covers the Apple II Expansion Card, FlexiDisk II, S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. The Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II are existing products presented alongside the three new interface/video cards. Cards initially use AION chips and include native Apple drivers and examples or supported S-100 CP/M adapters as appropriate. Keep host requirements and supplier support explicit.

Describe DRI’s software leadership and Logix’s hardware contribution. Invite independent computer, peripheral and software suppliers to a programme offering published specifications, versioning, backward-support policies, reference drivers, conformance tests, configuration diagnostics and a certification dispute process. Explain non-exclusive own-brand implementation, equal access to qualified components, disclosed supply priorities and manufacturer representation in a working group.

Identify the unresolved licence terms, reference-code redistribution rights, support duration and staffing, legacy-maintenance budget, working-group charter and voting rules, certification operator and scope, supply allocations, lead times and warranties. Present these as matters to settle, not existing contractual guarantees.

The 4 June 1979 announcement explains source migration and the planned optional Z80 compatibility path. Full architecture disclosure is scheduled for 19 May 1980. The all-years technical catalogue is internal author material, not a 1979 press kit.

Use the established Z80 C environment, documented APIs, portable file formats and separate platform adapters. A later target needs recompilation and testing, with review of assembly code, integer and pointer assumptions, memory banking and direct hardware access. Source portability does not preserve native Z80 binary execution.

Describe an optional Z80 coprocessor planned for qualified legacy applications. Availability and compatibility are not guaranteed for every model or hardware-dependent program. Keep its implementation, interconnect, memory mapping and host integration confidential until the architecture reveal.
Maintain CP/M tools and applications alongside next-generation development. Publish a funded support duration before making a dated service promise.
Explain that eight-bit computers retain useful business roles while falling costs broaden home, education and personal use. There is no fixed date when all business customers switch platforms.

The current professional digital monitor interface cannot drive a consumer television. A computer intended to use an existing television requires separate display engineering; the basic-storage configuration remains unresolved.

Invite suppliers to offer wider carriage, letter-quality printing, specialist forms and faster devices. Require the relevant status, character or graphics, paper and form-control support; the basic printer protocol does not cover every feature.
Invite business-chart and engineering-output devices, subject to a new plotting profile and suitable application support.
Invite communications and remote-access products with defined serial data, flow-control, modem-status and control profiles and host drivers.

Invite larger floppy systems, backup products and selected hard disks. Specify geometry, removable-media errors, durable writes, boot rules and measured throughput. Native faster disk controllers remain a valid choice.
Invite instruments, readers and business-input devices with published class or vendor-extension profiles and host drivers. Do not imply that foreign-processor ROM drivers execute automatically.

Document the actual file-transfer route and floppy formats used for the Aurelia-to-Model-II round trip. Publish tested RAM and application-workspace requirements, load and recalculation times and document-capacity limits. Label prepared data and recordings and preserve independent BPI branding and participant clearances.
Use booked presentation space; main-stage access, the exact slot and audiovisual suitability require confirmation. The eight presentation stages total 50 minutes, followed by questions.

Use this response to questions seeking confidential details: We will discuss the new architecture at NCC 1980. Today we can describe our C migration approach and planned optional Z80 compatibility path.

By the end of 1979, aim for Tandy shipping, one additional OEM selling a supported CP/M-extension or FlexiBUS configuration, another in qualification and verified third-party devices in several categories. By NCC 1980, aim for three to five distinct non-Logix manufacturers with supported configurations. Count Tandy once and exclude duplicate dealer builds and product variants; these are targets, not achieved results.

before.title: NCC 1979 open architecture and migration campaign — execution
before.description: Prepare the compatibility programme and partner demonstrations, deliver the NCC 1979 presentation and expansion-product launch, then run recruitment, dealer activity and qualification follow-up through the January 1980 review. Campaign.ncc1979 supplies the messages, presentation and marketing materials.

inputs.description: The Aurelia launch provides the working platform and business applications used to prepare cross-vendor demonstrations.
The Tandy cooperation agreement provides the basis for the Model II prototype and application-interchange work.
The limited Apple cooperation agreement provides documentation, test machines and compatibility assistance for native Apple II products.

Prepare named configurations, host-specific drivers, documented transfer paths and measured resource limits. Protect future architecture information and clear partner participation before public demonstrations.

outcomes.description: Published compatibility profiles, implementation guidance and records of unresolved access and support terms.
Rehearsed demonstration configurations, interoperability test records and an issue register distinguishing verified behaviour from limitations.
The NCC presentation and expansion-product launch have been delivered, with native Apple and S-100 support described separately and partner responsibilities retained.

An updated compatibility directory, recruitment and qualification records, dealer and developer materials, and an evidence-based closing review. Adoption and sales targets are not treated as achieved outcomes.

steps.description: Evaluate recruitment prospects and engineering kits. Prioritise North Star, with Lifeboat as a possible integration or distribution partner, then Vector Graphic. Preserve existing applications and display investment; interest does not constitute an agreement.

Treat North Star and Vector as strong CP/M prospects with moderately strong FlexiBUS prospects; optional Logix video is a moderate fit for North Star and a lower fit for Vector. Cromemco is a moderate CP/M and FlexiBUS prospect but a weak Logix-video prospect because of its own OS and graphics strategy. Altos is a moderately strong CP/M prospect with moderate FlexiBUS and limited Logix-video potential; no platform redesign is assumed. Intertec has moderately strong CP/M and moderate host-specific FlexiBUS potential, with limited Logix-video interest; plan late-1979 evaluation and possible 1980 qualification, not June availability. Heath/Heathkit has moderate CP/M and host-specific FlexiBUS potential but limited Logix-video interest; treat it as later feasibility work, not a promised 1979 release. These assessments guide outreach and do not establish commitments.
Publish compatibility profiles and provide reference-driver and test access alongside the separate DRI extension release. Record unresolved commercial and support terms.

Prepare the presentation space, audiovisual equipment and qualified demonstration systems. Test document round trips, disk formats, memory limits, loading, recalculation and device behaviour. Review all public material for the embargo and secure partner clearance.
Run supplier workshops, test named configurations and record failures and required corrections before public demonstrations.
Deliver the NCC presentation and the combined Apple II/S-100 expansion-product launch using the approved campaign materials and qualified systems.
Run dealer demonstrations, joint trade-press activity and developer clinics. Maintain a directory that distinguishes shipping, qualified and prototype configurations.
Update availability evidence for the separately recorded Tandy release and individually qualified SMC and peripheral products. Keep future products out of shipping claims.
Review progress against the campaign’s adoption targets using verified OEM configurations, qualifications and third-party device availability.

Track compatible-computer sell-through across vendors, qualified application editions, peripheral shipments and supported device classes, document-interchange results, support incidents, supplier concentration and component availability. Count distinct manufacturers rather than duplicate dealer builds or SKUs.

Prepare the closing review with verified customer examples, compatibility results and partner configurations. Report progress toward NCC 1980 goals without claiming unverified results or disclosing future architecture.

before.title: Model II software and interface cooperation
before.description: Develop and release the native-display Model II CP/M, Abacus and qualified FlexiBUS offering, then reinforce dealer training and integrated business bundles through 31 March 1980. Tandy retains its hardware platform and sales; its hardware revenue is not Logix revenue.

inputs.description: The cooperation must preserve the Model II native hardware architecture and satisfy its internal bus and host-interface constraints.

outcomes.description: Deliver the Model II CP/M and Abacus implementations and the qualified Model-II-specific FlexiBUS option while retaining Tandy’s existing host architecture. These outputs do not create the Model II computer or the FlexiBUS standard.
The released cooperation continues with reinforced business bundles and dealer training. Tandy’s independent hardware sales remain outside Logix revenue.

Agree the Model II compatibility design baseline and responsibilities.
Review prototype CP/M boot, native TUI, Abacus interchange, memory limits and the Model-II-specific FlexiBUS interface.
Announce the planned supported Model II CP/M, FlexiBUS and Abacus offering, distinguishing planned availability from completed sales.
Demonstrate the qualified Model II prototype at NCC while distinguishing demonstration from autumn customer release.
Release the supported Model II CP/M and Abacus configuration and separately qualified FlexiBUS option.
Reinforce native-video CP/M business bundles, dealer training and the existing cooperation after the customer release.

change.title: Phase 6: Place the November software presentation in COMDEX 1980
change.reason: Move the November Abacus 3/Pulse 3 presentation work out of the NCC campaign whose existing period ends in October, and consolidate it into the existing COMDEX 1980 execution process. Its existing start event already owns the 19 November launch; no second event, ownership edge or date change is needed. Preserve compatibility-progress and Aurelia-maintenance messages, but omit the obsolete forecast-specific revenue sentence from story activity text. Keep the unresolved Budget Hard-Disk Office composition/launch conflict for catalogue closeout; this proposal neither resolves it nor revises its product.

before.title: Artemis. A new generation. A familiar way to work. — execution
before.description: Communicate the launch, qualify demonstrations and coordinate follow-up described by the source campaign.

steps.description: activities / 1 / window: NCC 1980, May 19

activities / 1 / action: Live 55-minute keynote, independent BPI appearance after Abacus, benchmark method/results if measured, compatibility policy, software/configuration matrix and ordering sheets.
activities / 2 / window: Post-launch preparation leading to the 17 July 1980 Academy and regional-sales rollout

activities / 2 / action: Dealer demonstrations and customer workflow trials; press technical briefing; Academy transition classes and developer migration clinics; maintain issue/qualification register.
activities / 3 / window: 17 July–October 1980
